🚨 90-DAY NOTICE PERIOD? DON’T LET IT KILL YOUR NEXT JOB.
One of the biggest struggles for Indian IT professionals today is simple:
You cleared the interview.
The company wants you in 30 days.
Your current company says: “90 days.” 😓
This is still a real hiring friction point—Naukri even provides recruiters with notice-period-based candidate search because many hiring requirements prioritize people who can join quickly.
So, how should you handle it in 2026?
🔥 1. NEVER HIDE YOUR NOTICE PERIOD
Tell the recruiter upfront:
“My contractual notice period is 90 days. I can discuss an early-release option and will keep you updated.”
Don’t promise “I’ll join in 30 days” unless you actually have a realistic path to do it.
🤝 2. ASK FOR EARLY RELEASE WITH A PLAN
Don't simply say:
❌ “I want to leave early.”
Instead say:
✅ “I can complete KT, documentation, knowledge transfer and transition activities by X date. Could we discuss an early release?”
A clean handover gives your manager a practical reason to consider it.
💰 3. CHECK THE BUYOUT CLAUSE
Some employment contracts allow notice-pay/buyout for the unserved period, but you cannot assume that paying money automatically guarantees release; the contract and company policy matter, and employers may reject a buyout request.
🏖️ 4. CHECK LEAVE ADJUSTMENT
Ask HR whether accrued leave can be adjusted against the notice period. The answer depends on the company's policy and your contract.
📞 5. KEEP TALKING TO RECRUITERS
Don't stop your job search just because you have 60/90 days left.
Target companies that are willing to wait, and clearly communicate your actual last working day.
🎯 6. USE THE NOTICE PERIOD TO YOUR ADVANTAGE
Once you resign, don't mentally switch off.
Use those weeks to sharpen:
Playwright + API Testing + SQL + CI/CD + AI Testing
So when you join the next company, you're stronger than when you resigned.
💡 MY BIGGEST ADVICE
Don't fight your notice period emotionally.
Manage it strategically.
Read your contract.
Talk to HR.
Build a strong KT plan.
Discuss early release.
Understand buyout options.
Be transparent with the new employer.
Get every agreed change in writing.
And most importantly:
🚫 Never abscond just because another company is asking you to join quickly.
Your career transition should solve one problem without creating three new ones.

Share your experience—someone struggling with the same situation may find your comment useful. 🤝
General career guidance only; your employment contract, company policy and applicable law determine your specific situation.

The UK economy is growing. UK hiring is not. Both are true, and it's reshaping how smart companies recruit.
The latest Recruitonomics analysis by Julius Probst, PhD describes the market I'm seeing in client conversations every week: Julius Probst, PhD Julius interesting stats, thanks for the article. 

📈 GDP has grown at an annualised 2%+ in 2026, roughly 3x forecasts
📉 26,000 payroll jobs were lost in August, and ~220,000 since early 2024
🔍 Vacancies sit at ~700,000, the weakest hiring market since 2014 (pandemic aside)
⚖️ Unemployment is holding at ~4.9%
Why both are true: growth is concentrated in tech and professional services, where AI is lifting output. The job losses are in retail, hospitality and manufacturing, driven by cost pressures and the oil shock rather than AI.
What this means for hiring leaders:
→ Volume isn't the problem. Signal-to-noise is. Generalist roles attract floods of applicants, so screening becomes the bottleneck.
→ Scarcity is real where it matters. AI, data and cloud talent is short and pay is rising fast. Slow processes lose candidates.
→ Infrastructure talent is tightening as data-centre build-out accelerates.
→ With the Budget due next month, many firms are cautious on fixed headcount. Flexible capacity is worth more than ever.

How we're adapting at ALOIS Solutions UK:
✅ Building pipelines for AI, data and cloud skills before the requirement lands
✅ Rigorous screening, so hiring managers see shortlists, not inboxes
✅ Contract and flexible resourcing models that scale without long-term fixed cost
✅ Live market-rate insight, so offers land first time in fast-moving pay segments
In 2026, the challenge isn't filling roles. It's winning the candidates everyone else is chasing.

If you're planning Q4 or 2027 headcount and want a view on where UK talent is tight and where it's abundant, let's compare notes. My DMs are open.

What does an acquisition of Ascend + Galen Growth actually look like?

I've shared quite a bit about what we've built and why we believe the combined platforms are strategically interesting for certain personas (I'll name a few).

~Boutique all the way up to big 5 consulting firms with a healthcare vertical
~Venture studios and platforms that serve healthcare companies at scale
~Investors in all shapes and sizes
~Healthtech strategic that regularly launches products or has a big portfolio
~AI natives that want to launch a healthcare/life sciences services vertical

Now, maybe it's time to make the transaction itself a little less mysterious.

This is designed to be a relatively affordable strategic acquisition with several things already de-risked for a buyer.

 1️⃣ The IP is clean.
 2️⃣ The two platforms have already been integrated & optimized via MCP.
 3️⃣ There is a lightweight developer contract available to support technical transition and integration into the buyer's environment.
 4️⃣ The boards have endorsed a transaction floor.
 5️⃣ And importantly, an acquihire is absolutely on the table.

Who would you be hiring? Well, me for one 😇 . I've spent 25+ years building, commercializing and operating healthcare and health technology businesses and the last nine years I've been an Advisor to dozens of start-ups and strategics across our ecosystem. If the right buyer sees an opportunity not only in the assets, but in having me help integrate them, expand the use cases, build additional platforms or take the capability into market, I'm open to that conversation. I have several more people open as well.

That doesn't have to be part of the transaction. Some organizations will already have the product, technical and commercial capabilities they need. 
Some buyers may even want ANIE more than HealthTech Alpha or vice versa, that's fine.

Others may look at what we've built and see the foundation for something considerably larger, but not have the internal healthcare commercialization expertise or resources to immediately turn it into that.

We can solve for these scenarios.

That's one of the things I find particularly compelling about this opportunity. 

A buyer doesn't need to take on a large organization or significant operating infrastructure to acquire the capability.

They can acquire the assets, integrate them into what they already do and run or they can acquire the foundation and some of the people and knowledge needed to build on top of it.

The capital required isn't intended to be the barrier here either, w/ NDA we will share base price for the combo or each set of assets priced separately.

The real question is whether the right organization can look at the integrated platforms, the IP, the intelligence and the opportunity ahead and see something they could make considerably more valuable inside their business.

If you do, let's talk.

We're making this an easy acquisition to execute.

AI will not “take over digital programs in a year.”
Organizations can hand them over. Those are not the same claim.

The one-year forecast keeps circulating because a few lab CEOs said models would write most—or all—of the code, and the headline traveled farther than the caveat. In some startups and AI labs, that is already directionally true: models draft a large share of new code, open pull requests, and run tests. That is a change in how software is produced. It is not a machine seizing the stack.

Three distinctions matter.
Capability is not custody.
A model can generate a service. It cannot approve production access, sign a vendor contract, accept liability, or rewrite a regulated system unless a human grants those rights.
“AI wrote the code” is not “AI owns the program.”
Humans still define the product, constraints, architecture, security posture, and acceptable risk. When those steps are skipped, the failure is governance, not inevitability.
Adoption is a policy choice.

Firms choose to buy agents, grant repository access, weaken review, cut junior hiring, and treat speed as a substitute for accountability. Highly regulated domains already refuse that bargain. Others can refuse it too.

The serious risk is narrower than takeover mythology. If leaders give agents write access, production credentials, and thin review, effective control can drift while humans remain formally in charge. That is still a human design decision: how much autonomy to grant, what must be audited, and who is liable when the generated system fails.

Ethical AI leadership is not predicting the calendar. It is deciding what may act without a named owner.

If your organization is widening agent autonomy this quarter, the question is not “Will AI take over?”
It is: Who remains accountable when it ships?

In January, Thomson Reuters emphasized the need for tempered optimism around legal demand growth last year because it occurred amid changes in client power, economic and geopolitical conditions and AI advancements. At the same time, a Major, Lindsey & Africa report this year highlighted how this background of change and uncertainty has driven sustained demand for contract talent and interim counsel.

As profits have been fueled by this volatility, firms have reason to be cautious about investing in full-time hires. Freelancer vs Contract AI talent, what’s actually the difference?
 
The terms are often used interchangeably, but they can represent very different ways of working.
 
A freelancer typically works independently across specific tasks or projects, often with multiple clients and a high degree of flexibility.
A contract professional, on the other hand, is usually engaged for a defined role, project, or period — with clearer responsibilities, deliverables, and timelines.
 
For companies hiring AI talent, the distinction matters.
The right engagement model depends on what you’re trying to build:
→ Need specialized expertise for a focused task?
 → Need someone to support a larger AI project for several months?
 → Need flexibility without committing to a permanent role?
Understanding the difference helps companies structure AI teams around the work that actually needs to get done.
Because hiring AI talent isn't just about who you hire.
It’s also about how you engage them.

AI regulation in the United States is not one law.

It is a patchwork.

And that patchwork is getting harder for organizations to ignore.

While the EU AI Act gets most of the global attention, U.S. state-level privacy and AI laws are already creating real obligations for companies using automated decision-making, biometric data, hiring tools, profiling, or high-risk AI systems.

California, Colorado, Illinois, and New York City are good examples of where the pressure is increasing.

California's CCPA and CPRA focus on consumer privacy rights, including access, deletion, correction, opt-out, and limits on sensitive personal information.

Colorado's AI Act introduces obligations for high-risk AI systems involved in consequential decisions such as employment, lending, housing, insurance, healthcare, and similar areas.

Illinois BIPA remains one of the most serious biometric privacy laws, requiring informed consent, retention controls, and deletion obligations.

New York City Local Law 144 requires bias audits and transparency for automated employment decision tools.

The common themes are clear:

1. Consumers must know when and how their data is used  
2. Sensitive and biometric data need stronger consent and protection  
3. Automated decisions need transparency and, in many cases, human review  
4. High-risk AI systems require impact assessments and ongoing monitoring  
5. Vendors and third-party AI tools must be contractually controlled  
6. Organizations must maintain evidence, not just policies  

For legal and compliance teams, the discussion should start with practical questions:

Which AI systems are already in production?

Which states do our users, employees, applicants, or customers come from?

Do we use AI for hiring, lending, insurance, healthcare, education, profiling, or eligibility decisions?

Do we collect biometric, sensitive, behavioral, or inferred personal data?

Do our privacy notices actually explain automated decision-making?

Can users access, correct, delete, or opt out where required?

Do we have a human review path for consequential decisions?

Do vendor contracts include data-use limits, audit rights, retention rules, and compliance obligations?

Do we have evidence of bias testing, impact assessments, and monitoring?

The biggest risk is not only regulatory fines.

It is discovering too late that "AI innovation" has been running without legal visibility, data governance, vendor control, or audit evidence.

🌍 The Core Economic Tension: "Low-Hiring, Low-Firing" Caution
The global economy is currently defined by a high-stakes standoff between resilient macroeconomic growth and severe structural policy uncertainty. 

UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD)
 +4
Major organizations are navigating a unique "low-hiring, low-firing" equilibrium. Mass layoffs have slowed, but companies are highly reluctant to expand their baseline operations. 
🎯 The Current Intentions of Recruiters & Employers
Because of this cautious macroeconomic environment, the motivations, targets, and operational styles of recruitment teams have fundamentally shifted by four main intentions:
1. Strategic:
The Target: Recruiters are hyper-focused on candidates with technical proficiencies that drive immediate revenue or immense productivity gains—specifically AI integration, machine learning, data science, and cybersecurity. 
2. Demanding "CEO-Level" Justification for Every Single Hire:
The Reality: Because recruiters risk their own internal reputation if a hire fails, they are dragging out the interview process. 
3. Shifting Toward Temporary, Gig, and Fractional Talent
The Strategy: Recruiters are actively building networks of specialized freelancers and contingent workers who can execute short-term projects and be scaled down instantly if the economy dips.
4. Targeting High-Value "Passive" Candidates
The Focus: Recruiters are purposefully hunting "passive candidates"—professionals who are currently securely employed and not looking for work. 
📊 Recruiter Focus: Perm vs. Contract Roles
